text: A site-to-site VPN connects an entire on-prem network to a cloud VNet or VPC, so every device on either side can reach the other over private IP addresses, subject to firewall rules. It does this over the public internet, wrapped in an encrypted IPsec tunnel -- not over the cloud provider's own private backbone. That distinction matters more than it sounds like it should.

This is the key difference from VNet peering, which you saw earlier in this path. Peering connects two cloud networks to each other over Azure's or AWS's own backbone and never touches the internet. Site-to-site VPN exists because the on-prem side isn't in the cloud at all, so there's no backbone available to put it on -- the tunnel has to cross the public internet like any other traffic, and IPsec encryption and authentication are what keep that trip confidential and tamper-resistant.

Each side needs a gateway pair before any traffic can flow. In Azure, a VPN Gateway sits in the VNet's dedicated GatewaySubnet, paired with a Local Network Gateway resource that just describes the on-prem side -- its public IP address and the address ranges behind it. AWS uses the same idea under different names: a Virtual Private Gateway attached to the VPC, and a Customer Gateway describing the on-prem device. A Connection resource ties the pair together with a shared key or certificate.

Both clouds provision the connection as two tunnels by default, each terminating on a different physical endpoint on the provider's side. That means one tunnel can go down for scheduled maintenance or an unexpected hardware failure without taking the whole connection with it -- but the on-prem device has to be configured to accept both tunnels and actively fail over between them, not just rely on whichever one it finds first.

Site-to-site VPN is cheap and fast to stand up -- often hours, not weeks -- but it's still riding the public internet underneath the encryption, with whatever latency variability that implies. Next up: Azure ExpressRoute and AWS Direct Connect, the dedicated-circuit alternative that skips the public internet entirely.
